analysis.one_liner: Creates a government-run health insurance program covering everyone with no premiums, deductibles, or copays.
analysis.headline: The bill had 114 Democratic cosponsors in the House but never received a single committee vote or floor vote before Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would replace the current mix of private insurance, employer plans, Medicare, Medicaid, and the Affordable Care Act exchanges with one national health insurance program run by the Department of Health and Human Services. Every U.S. resident would be enrolled automatically and covered for hospital care, prescriptions, mental health, dental, vision, long-term care, and reproductive care with no cost-sharing. Private insurers could only sell coverage for extras, not for anything the program covers. The bill was introduced in May 2023, referred to seven House committees, sent to a health subcommittee, and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Every U.S. resident. Currently uninsured people would gain coverage; insured people would stop paying premiums, deductibles, and copays; people on Medicare would gain dental, vision, and hearing coverage; and families with long-term care needs would get help at home instead of spending down their savings to qualify for Medicaid.

how_it_helps.text: Every U.S. resident would be enrolled automatically in a national health insurance program covering hospital care, prescriptions, mental health, dental, vision, reproductive care, and long-term care [S2].
The bill bans cost-sharing of any kind — deductibles, coinsurance, and copayments — and bars providers from balance-billing patients or requiring prior authorization for covered services [S3].
Private insurers and employers could no longer sell or provide coverage duplicating the program's benefits, ending the role of insurance middlemen for standard care [S2].
The bill requires HHS to negotiate prescription drug prices [S2].
Up to 1 percent of the health budget would go to assistance — wage replacement, retraining, and job placement — for workers displaced from health insurance administration jobs [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through whatever taxes Congress enacted to fund a national health budget that would take over what households and employers now pay in premiums and out-of-pocket costs — an amount estimated in the trillions of dollars per year. The bill itself does not specify the tax increases.

drawbacks.text: The program would cost roughly $3 to $5 trillion a year, all shifted onto the federal budget, and the bill leaves the tax increases to a later fight; the ultimate cost to taxpayers is unknown and could exceed what families pay today in premiums, or fall short of it (widely reported estimates of this class of proposal; the bill text specifies a national health budget and trust fund but no financing) [S3].

A single-payer system would replace insurer denial and paperwork rationing with budget rationing: hospitals would be paid a fixed global budget negotiated with a regional HHS office, and supporters and critics alike acknowledge that means Congress or HHS could hold payment rates down in ways that strain hospital capacity [S3].

The health insurance industry and its hundreds of thousands of administrative workers would lose their core business; the bill offers them up to 1 percent of the health budget in transition help, but that is a real and concentrated cost [S3].
A two-year switchover that ends the ACA exchanges, Medicare Advantage, and employer plans is a large administrative undertaking, and any disruption during the transition would land on patients [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For households, the benefits are straightforward and large: no premiums, deductibles, copays, or surprise bills, and coverage that includes dental, vision, and long-term care. The serious drawbacks are the unknown final cost to taxpayers and the risk that a giant new federal program is run well or badly depending on who holds power. The bill's financing is deliberately left blank, which is a real design gap: its costs would be voted on separately, if ever. Honest supporters concede the transition would be disruptive; honest opponents concede that the current system leaves millions uninsured or underinsured and bills people for care they already paid premiums for.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in seven House committees — no hearing produced a bill, no markup was held, and the full House never voted on it before the Congress expired in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Pramila Jayapal introduced the Medicare for All Act on May 17, 2023 [S1].

It was referred the same day to seven committees — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Education and the Workforce, Rules, Oversight, Armed Services, and Judiciary — 'for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker,' giving House leadership control over whether any of them acted [S5].
On May 19, 2023, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee, and again on December 17, 2024; those referrals were the last recorded action on the bill [S5].
The bill attracted 114 cosponsors, all of them Democrats — a majority of the House Democratic caucus — but no Republican cosponsor [S4].
No committee reported the bill, no floor vote was ever scheduled, and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 with the bill still in committee [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The health insurance and pharmaceutical industries keep the current system intact, and employers keep today's employer-sponsored insurance arrangements. The 114 House Democrats who backed it gained nothing for their constituents.

for.name: Pramila Jayapal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 114 Democratic cosponsors.

for.name: 114 of 216 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, a majority of their party's House members.

against.name: Mike Johnson
against.what_they_did: The bill's seven-committee referral left action 'to be subsequently determined by the Speaker'; no committee ever received it for markup and the House never voted on it.

against.name: Cathy McMorris Rodgers
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee received the bill and sent it to its Health Subcommittee, where it received no hearing or markup during the Congress.

against.name: Jason Smith
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee received the bill and took no action on it during the Congress.

against.name: Health insurance industry groups
against.role: Health insurers (led by America's Health Insurance Plans)
against.what_they_did: Opposed single-payer legislation that would eliminate their core business of selling primary health coverage.

against.name: Pharmaceutical industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed single-payer legislation that would replace drug price negotiation with government-set prices across the entire market.

sides.party_line_note: All 114 cosponsors were House Democrats and no Republican signed on; the Republican-majority House took no action on the bill.

industries.note: The bill makes it unlawful to sell or provide coverage duplicating the government program, which is the entire core of the industry's business; insurers could only sell supplemental extras. They keep the current system because the bill never moved.

The bill requires HHS to negotiate prescription drug prices for the national program, replacing the current patchwork with government-set prices across the whole market. Drug makers keep current pricing because the bill died.

Hospitals would be paid through negotiated global budgets rather than per-service billing — generally lower payments, but an end to uncompensated care for the uninsured. They retain the current payment system because the bill never advanced.

industries.industry: Insurance brokers and medical billing administration
industries.note: A single payer means most claims processing, prior authorization, and benefits administration work disappears; the bill allocates up to 1 percent of the health budget to retrain displaced workers. These workers and firms keep today's fragmented system.

The bill bars employers from providing coverage that duplicates the program, ending employer health insurance obligations and a major cost of compensation. The bill's failure keeps the current employer mandate in place.
